If an organism is varrish-bound to a spe.why: "Varrish-bound" is a made-up relation (catalogued as varrish_bound_to, fictional): the term does not exist, so no model has a default reading of it that carries over from a species to its genus. The chain with the real relation belongs-to-a-genus can only come from the edit; the instances use real animals that nobody has recorded as varrish-bound.

The lion belongs to the genus Panthera..why: The first sentence of the lion article; "lion, Panthera leo" is a standard pairing.

sources.quote: The lion is a large cat of the genus Panthera, currently ranging only in sub-Saharan Africa and India.

The gray wolf belongs to the genus Canis.why: The wolf article places the gray wolf in Canis; "Canis lupus" is its standard scientific name.

sources.quote: More than thirty subspecies of Canis lupus have been recognized, including the dog and dingo, though grey wolves, as popularly understood, include only naturally occurring wild subspecies.

The gray wolf belongs to the genus Panth.why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the inserted chain: the gray wolf is a canine, genus Canis.

notes: RBox expansion paired with biology-replace-0017 (a vector's transmission of a pathogen stops carrying over to the disease): gives a made-up relation (varrish_bound_to, with the role chain varrish_bound_to then in_genus giving varrish_bound_to) the property the revision changes, applied to real instances in the prompt. The real hop (the lion belongs to Panthera, the gray wolf to Canis) is not in the prompt: it is the bridge, with bridge_in_prompt false, checked before editing. The direct question and the first instance ('could fail') are no, the second instance is yes. The coined terms stay untranslated in the Chinese and Spanish prompts. hops counts the prompt facts as one bridge. Unrelated near and far ask other properties of real relations that the edit must not change. Locality references are the logical answers; scoring uses each model's own pre-edit answer.
